stimulus.text:
“'Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land,
Taught my benighted soul to understand
That there's a God, that there's a Saviour too:
Once I redemption neither sought nor knew.
Some view our sable race with scornful eye,
‘Their colour is a diabolic die.’
Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain,
May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train.”
— Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America,” in Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773)
stimulus.source_note: Phillis Wheatley, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773). Public domain.

stem: The publication of Wheatley's book of poems in London in 1773 was remarkable mainly because

options.text: Poetry was illegal to print in the British colonies
options.misconception: Poetry was legal; Boston had presses and poets, so the genre was never the obstacle.

options.text: Boston had no printing presses that could print a book
options.misconception: Boston had presses; her book was printed in London because no Boston publisher would take it, not because presses were missing.

options.text: Women were barred by law from publishing any writing
options.misconception: No law barred women from publishing; the barrier Wheatley broke was literacy and a public voice for an enslaved person.

options.text: Enslaved people were systematically denied literacy and a public voice

rationales.D: Background: enslaved people were systematically denied literacy and a public voice, so a book of poems by an enslaved woman startled readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
rationales.A: Poetry was not illegal; the remarkable thing was who wrote the poems, not the genre.
rationales.B: Boston had printing presses; the book went to London because publishers there took it up.
rationales.C: Women did publish in the colonies; the barrier was slavery's ban on Black literacy and voice.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what was unusual. Not the poems, but the poet: an enslaved Black woman.
2. Ask what stood in her way. Background: slavery's ban on literacy and on a public voice for enslaved people.
3. Drop the false barriers. Background: poetry was legal, Boston had presses, and women did publish.
Remember: when a first is famous, ask what rule it broke — the person, not the product, is the story.
